blocks.text: Not every MCP server lives on a distant machine.
A huge share of real world servers run right alongside the host, launched as a subprocess the moment they are needed.
This lesson looks at exactly that pattern, the local server, and why it is such a natural fit for developer tools.
1. What Makes a Server Local
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440481843-172108232.png
A local server runs on the exact same machine as the host that talks to it.
It is typically launched as a subprocess, started when the session begins and stopped when it ends, rather than running continuously as its own independent service.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If shutting down the host would also make sense to shut down the server, it is very likely a local server.

blocks.text: Nothing about the MCP protocol itself changes based on this choice, only where the process actually lives.
2. STDIO Is the Natural Transport Here
Because a local server is just a subprocess, its standard input and output are already directly available to the host.
This is exactly why stdio, covered in its own dedicated lesson, is the default transport choice for local servers, no network stack needed at all.

code.content:
import subprocess
process = subprocess.Popen(
    ["python", "file_server.py"],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
)

blocks.text: Nothing prevents a local server from using a different transport, but stdio remains by far the simplest, lowest overhead option available.
3. A Simpler Trust Model
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440481843-214207343.png
A local server runs as the same user, on the same machine, as the host itself.

There is no network boundary to cross, which removes an entire category of authentication concerns that a remote server has to solve, the operating system process boundary does a lot of the work implicitly.

code.content:
# the operating system already enforces this boundary
# a process cannot read another user's files without explicit permission

blocks.text: That said, this simplicity should never be mistaken for a guarantee, careful design still matters.
4. Common Use Cases for Local Servers
File system access, running local shell commands, reading a local git repository, these are classic local server tasks.
Each one only makes sense in the context of one specific machine, the one the user is actually sitting at.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Use case","Why local fits"],"rows":[["File access","Files live on this machine"],["Running shell commands","The shell only exists here"],["Local git operations","The repository is on disk here"]]}

blocks.text: None of these tasks would make sense running on someone else machine entirely.
5. Starting and Stopping the Server Process
The host is responsible for launching the server process when a session begins.
When the session ends, the host also terminates that process, tying the server lifetime directly to the session lifetime covered in the MCP Fundamentals module.
This tight coupling is deliberate, a local server has no reason to keep running once nothing is left to talk to it.
6. What Happens if the Process Crashes

blocks.alt: What Happens if the Process Crashes
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440481844-666653596.png
A local server crashing looks, from the host side, like the subprocess exiting unexpectedly.
A well built host detects this, treats any pending requests as failed, and can optionally offer to restart the server automatically.
Logging the exit code and any final output the process produced makes diagnosing the crash afterward much easier.
A restart should also reset any assumptions the client made about server state, since the new process starts fresh.
7. File System Access Without a Network Round Trip

blocks.alt: File System Access Without a Network Round Trip
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440481844-865725906.png
A local file system server can read and write files with essentially no latency, since nothing ever leaves the machine.
This is one of the clearest performance advantages a local server has over an equivalent remote one.

code.content:
# no network call involved, just local disk access
with open(path) as f:
    content = f.read()

blocks.text: 8. Permissions Still Matter Locally
Being local does not mean being automatically safe.
A local server with unrestricted file system access can still do real damage if a tool call goes wrong, scoping what it can touch, covered in the Sandboxing lesson, remains important.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A local trust boundary answers who is calling, it says nothing about whether a specific action should actually be allowed.

blocks.text: The Sandboxing lesson later in this curriculum covers exactly how to enforce that scoping in practice.
9. Distributing a Local Server
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440482132-668383462.png
A local server is typically packaged as a small, installable program, a script, a compiled binary, or a package published to a language specific registry.
A user installs it once, and any compatible host can then launch it as needed.
Popular package managers, appropriate to whatever language the server is written in, are the most common distribution channel.

blocks.title: A practical tip
blocks.content: Pinning a specific tested version in installation instructions avoids the it works on my machine problem across different users.

blocks.text: 10. Local Servers and Multiple Hosts
The same installed local server binary can be launched by several different host applications on the same machine.
Each host starts its own separate subprocess instance, they do not share a running server between them.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Local server","Remote server"],"rows":[["Where it runs","Same machine as the host","A separate machine or service"],["Typical transport","stdio","HTTP or WebSocket"],["Trust model","Process boundary","Network authentication"]]}

blocks.text: This is exactly the same one client per server principle covered in the MCP Architecture module, just applied at the process level here.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If two hosts each launch their own copy of the same server binary, they are not sharing state unless the server itself was built to persist data to disk.

blocks.text: 11. When a Local Server Is the Wrong Choice

blocks.alt: When a Local Server Is the Wrong Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440482132-449943783.png
A local server cannot serve multiple users at once, or scale beyond one machine.
Anything that needs to be shared across many users, or accessed from devices other than the one it runs on, belongs on a remote server instead.
A multi user support ticket system, for example, clearly needs to run centrally rather than on any one individual machine.
12. Version Management for Local Servers
An installed local server can drift out of date if a user never updates it.
Some hosts check for a newer version at launch time, or bundle a specific known good version directly, to avoid depending on whatever happens to already be installed.
Bundling removes an entire class of compatibility bugs caused by mismatched versions in the wild.
13. Debugging a Local Server Directly
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440482133-130532500.png
Because a local server is just a regular process, it can be run and tested completely outside of any host, directly from a terminal.
This makes debugging noticeably easier than debugging a server buried inside a remote deployment.

code.content:
# running a local server manually from a terminal for testing
$ python file_server.py
# then sending raw JSON-RPC messages by hand to inspect its behavior

blocks.text: Many developers write their first MCP server this way, testing it by hand before ever wiring it into a real host.
14. A Worked Example
Trace a host launching a local file system server and reading a project file through it.

code.content:
process = subprocess.Popen(["mcp-fs-server"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
client = MCPClient(transport=StdioTransport(process))
client.initialize()
content = client.read_resource("file:///project/README.md")

blocks.text: If the process crashed partway through, the host would detect the closed pipe and could offer to relaunch it automatically.
15. Common Mistakes When Using Local Servers

items: Assuming a local server needs no permission scoping just because it is not exposed to the network.
Forgetting to terminate the subprocess when a session ends, leaving orphaned processes running.
Never handling an unexpected process crash, leaving pending requests stuck forever.
Trying to share one local server instance across multiple unrelated hosts instead of launching separate instances.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is assuming a local server never needs updating, stale installed versions can miss important fixes.
A sixth common mistake is not testing what happens when the server binary is simply missing or fails to launch at all.
16. Practice: Launch Your Own Local Server
Sketch the code a host would use to launch a simple local server, wire it up over stdio, and cleanly terminate it once the session ends.

code.content:
try:
    client.initialize()
    # use the session
finally:
    process.terminate()

blocks.text: Extend this sketch to also detect and log an unexpected process exit before the session was meant to end.
Key Takeaway

A local server runs as a subprocess on the same machine as its host, typically over stdio, with a simpler trust model than a remote server, ideal for tasks tied to one specific machine like file access or local commands.
This lesson pairs directly with Remote MCP Servers from earlier in this module, together they cover the two fundamental deployment shapes an MCP server can take.

The debugging advantage covered in the newly added section is one of the most practical, everyday benefits of building a local server, testing it never requires a full host application, just a terminal.
